title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Overview
body:
Global Transaction Consistency Database is a capability database for global transaction consistency. Global transaction consistency makes a change that touches several stores either succeed everywhere or fail everywhere, so readers never see a half-applied update.

The capability rests on two-phase commit, participant voting, atomic commit or abort, recovery after failure. Each of these ideas is explained in plain sentences in the records that follow, so a reader can understand what the capability does before studying how it would be built.

This database holds ten full records: an overview, a core design, an architecture, a working demo with its analysis, an implementation status, tests and validation, related capabilities, limits and safeguards, and a roadmap. This public edition records established design principles for this capability. The status record states the honest position in full: implementation_status is designed: the design and a working demo of the capability logic exist here. Network-wide deployment of this capability is planned, not claimed as live. The demo proves the logic, not a network deployment.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Core Design
body:
The core design of global transaction consistency starts from one plain rule: Global transaction consistency makes a change that touches several stores either succeed everywhere or fail everywhere, so readers never see a half-applied update.

The design is organised around two-phase commit, participant voting, atomic commit or abort, recovery after failure. Inputs enter through a stated entry point, are checked against stated rules, and leave as a checked result with a record of what happened, so any later reader can retrace the decision.

Nothing in the core design depends on hidden behaviour. Every rule that affects an outcome is named in the design, every limit is stated as a number, and every failure path ends in a report rather than silence. This public edition records established design principles for this capability.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Architecture
body:
The architecture of global transaction consistency has three layers. The first layer accepts work and checks that it is well formed. The second layer applies the capability logic, using two-phase commit, participant voting, atomic commit or abort, recovery after failure. The third layer records results, reports failures, and exposes the outcome for review.

Each layer can be tested on its own, and each layer keeps its own log, so a fault in one layer does not silently corrupt the others. State is kept explicit, with no step relying on a value that was never written down.

Scaling is handled by the same rules at any size: the same checks, the same limits, and the same reporting apply whether the workload is ten items or ten thousand, and the architecture states where it would need more capacity before it is asked to carry more. This public edition records established design principles for this capability.

The demo was executed at build time, and the output stored with this record is the real captured output of that run, not a hand-written expectation. Running the same code again produces the same output, because the demo uses fixed inputs and no randomness.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Demo Analysis
body:
The demo for global transaction consistency proves that the core decision can be expressed as clear code with observable output: inputs go in, the stated rule is applied, and a checkable result comes out.

What the demo does not prove is equally important. It does not prove performance at network scale, it does not prove behaviour under real production load or failure, and it does not prove that any live system in the network already uses this capability. Those claims would need separate evidence, and none is claimed here.

Read the demo as a logic check and a teaching tool: a correct miniature of the idea, honestly bounded. This public edition records established design principles for this capability.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Implementation Status
body:
Implementation status for Global Transaction Consistency Database: designed. The design in this database exists, and the working demo of the capability logic exists and was executed at build time.

Network-wide deployment is planned, not claimed as live. No record in this database states that the whole network now runs this capability, and no reader should take the existence of this design database as evidence of deployment.

The path from designed to deployed is laid out in the roadmap record: staged trials, measured results, and a deployment decision based on evidence from those trials, not on the existence of this document.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Tests and Validation
body:
Tests for global transaction consistency start with the demo itself: fixed inputs, deterministic output, and a stored output that later runs must match exactly. Any change to the logic that changes the output must be explained, not hidden.

Further tests check the edges: empty input, a single item, an item at exactly the stated limit, and an item just beyond it. Each edge case has an expected outcome written before the test runs, and a test that fails stops the release of that change until the failure is understood.

Validation also checks the records themselves: every record is full prose, every identifier is unique, every demo output matches a fresh run, and no record claims a deployment that has not happened.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Related Capabilities and Cross-Links
body:
Global Transaction Consistency connects to neighbouring capabilities in this lane. Distributed index federation, automatic shard placement, backpressure scheduling, resource-aware generation, storage tiers, synchronization, and transaction consistency form the data-platform group. Specialist selection, evidence-weighted synthesis, delegation negotiation, and human approval escalation form the coordination group. Typed, constraint-aware, dependency-aware, incremental, scored, novelty-checked, lifecycle-managed, self-repairing, quota-controlled, and safeguard-bounded generation form the generation group.

Cross-links run in both directions: this capability may depend on a neighbour, and a neighbour may depend on this one. The records name those directions plainly, so a builder can follow the chain without guessing which link is a dependency and which is merely related.

No cross-link in this database is a claim about another system. Each link points to a capability design in the same lane, and the reader can open that database and judge its own status record on the same honest terms.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Limits, Risks and Safeguards
body:
The limits of global transaction consistency are stated, not discovered by accident. The design works within stated sizes, stated budgets, and stated time bounds, and it refuses or reports rather than silently degrading when those bounds are reached.

Risks include misconfiguration, stale state, and over-trust in a demo that is only a miniature. Safeguards against those risks are explicit: stated limits, checked outputs, audit records of decisions, human review where risk is high, and a stop rule that halts work rather than letting a fault spread.

This database is defensive and design-only in its security aspects: it describes detection, checking, ordering, and resistance to faults, and it contains no instructions for attacking, defeating, or undermining any system.

title: Global Transaction Consistency Database: Roadmap to Full Implementation
body:
The roadmap from designed to deployed for global transaction consistency proceeds in stages. First, the design and demo in this database are reviewed for correctness and clarity. Second, a small staged trial runs the logic on real but bounded work, with measured results kept as evidence.

Third, the trial results decide whether to widen the trial, revise the design, or stop. Widening happens only on positive measured evidence, and each widening keeps the same checks, limits, and reporting that the trial used.

Full implementation is declared only when staged evidence supports it, at which point the status record would be updated by a new, evidenced record. Until then, the honest status remains designed, and this database continues to say so plainly.
